nameStory: This little speedwell gets its name from its tiny leaves that look remarkably like those of thyme - the herb you might have in your kitchen spice rack. The "speedwell" part comes from an old tradition of travelers tucking these flowers into their clothing for good luck and safe travels, with "speed you well" being a common farewell blessing.
description: Thyme-leaved speedwell is a low-growing perennial that forms creeping mats along the ground, rarely reaching more than 4-6 inches tall. It produces delicate spikes of tiny pale blue or white flowers with darker blue stripes, each flower smaller than your pinky nail. The small, oval leaves are arranged opposite each other along creeping stems that root at the nodes, creating dense carpets in suitable spots. This humble little plant is one of our most common speedwells, quietly spreading across lawns, paths, and disturbed areas.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny pale blue or white flowers with darker blue stripes, arranged in loose spikes at stem tips. Each flower has four petals and is barely 1/8 inch across - you'll need to get down close to appreciate their delicate beauty.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small, oval leaves arranged in opposite pairs along the stem, resembling miniature thyme leaves. They feel smooth and slightly succulent, with a fresh, mild scent when crushed between your fingers.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low, creeping mats that hug the ground, with stems that root at joints where they touch soil. The whole plant feels soft and cushiony underfoot, like a living carpet.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Tiny heart-shaped seed capsules that split open when ripe, each containing numerous microscopic seeds. The capsules are so small you might need a magnifying glass to see their distinctive shape clearly.

habitat: Look for thyme-leaved speedwell in disturbed soils, lawn edges, garden paths, and along roadsides throughout New England. It thrives in moist, compacted soils where other plants struggle, often appearing in the spaces between stepping stones or along the margins of driveways. You'll find it from sea level to moderate elevations, typically in areas with some foot traffic or soil disturbance.

seasonality.spring: Flowers begin appearing in late April and May, with the plant emerging from winter as small green mats. This is peak blooming season when the tiny blue flowers are most abundant and easiest to spot.
seasonality.summer: Continues flowering through summer, though less prolifically than in spring. The creeping stems actively spread and root, extending the plant's coverage across suitable areas.
seasonality.fall: Flowering tapers off but doesn't completely stop, with scattered blooms possible into October. The foliage remains green and the plant continues growing slowly in mild weather.
seasonality.winter: Persists as evergreen mats under snow, with leaves turning slightly purplish in cold weather. The low-growing habit helps it survive winter traffic and harsh conditions that kill other plants.

funFact: This tiny speedwell is actually a botanical detective's dream - it's one of the few plants that can tell you exactly how compacted your soil is, thriving in earth so hard-packed that earthworms avoid it, yet disappearing once the soil becomes fluffy and well-aerated.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other small speedwells, but thyme-leaved speedwell's creeping, mat-forming habit sets it apart from the more upright corn speedwell or the larger-flowered Germander speedwell. Remember: if it's making a carpet and the leaves really do look like tiny thyme leaves, you've found your plant.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its common appearance in disturbed areas, this isn't necessarily a "weed" to despise - it's actually performing valuable ecological services by preventing soil erosion and providing early nectar for small pollinators when few other flowers are available.
compareHints: Among New England's speedwells, thyme-leaved speedwell is unique in its strongly creeping, mat-forming habit - most other speedwells grow more upright. Its tiny thyme-like leaves are smaller and more succulent-feeling than those of heath speedwell, and its growth pattern is much more prostrate than the trailing but upward-angled stems of Germander speedwell.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's speedwells, heath speedwell is unique for its distinctly creeping, mat-forming growth habit and very fuzzy stems and leaves.
Among the speedwells, germander speedwell stands out for having the brightest blue flowers and the most prominent flower stalks that clearly rise above the foliage.
Among the speedwells, corn speedwell is distinguished by its fuzzy leaves and very small size - it's one of the tiniest in the genus.
Among the speedwells, marsh speedwell is distinctive for its wetland habitat and very narrow leaves.
Bird's-eye speedwell stands out from its many speedwell relatives by having the brightest, most intensely blue flowers with the most prominent dark radiating lines.
Among the many speedwells in New England, American brooklime is the water-lover of the group.
Among New England's many speedwell species, purslane speedwell stands out for its highly variable leaf shapes on a single plant and its preference for the most disturbed habitats.
Unlike the upright thyme-leaved speedwell or the larger-flowered Germander speedwell, slender speedwell stays flat to the ground with its characteristic thread-thin stems.

Long-leaved Speedwell towers over most other New England speedwells - while species like Thyme-leaved Speedwell hug the ground and Germander Speedwell stays low in lawns, this species stands tall with substantial flower spikes.
Unlike most other New England speedwells that are annual weeds or die back completely in winter, creeping speedwell is a true perennial that forms permanent mats.

Among New England speedwells, broadleaf speedwell stands out for its relatively large, oval leaves and dense flower spikes - most other speedwells have much smaller, narrower leaves and more open flower arrangements.
Among New England's many speedwells, blue water-speedwell is unique in its aquatic lifestyle - while American brooklime also likes wet areas, it grows taller and has larger flowers.
Among New England's speedwells, ivy-leaved speedwell is easily distinguished by its distinctive lobed leaves that look like tiny ivy leaves.
Unlike its lowland speedwell relatives that grow in fields and gardens, American alpine speedwell is the mountain specialist of the family.
Spiked speedwell towers over its New England speedwell relatives, most of which are small, creeping, or prostrate plants with much smaller flower clusters.
Among the many speedwells in New England, Pink Ivy-leaved Speedwell stands out for its distinctly lobed, ivy-like leaves - most other speedwells have simple, unlobed leaves.
Grey field-speedwell stands out from its speedwell relatives primarily by its grayish leaf color and extremely small size.
Among the speedwells, chain speedwell is unique for its strong preference for aquatic habitats and its creeping, often floating growth habit.
